data.title: Rapamycin causes regression of astrocytomas in tuberous sclerosis complex
data.authors: Franz DN; Leonard J; Tudor C; Chuck G; Care M; Sethuraman G; Dinopoulos A; Thomas G; Crone KR

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Humans: case series of 5 patients with TSC (4 subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, 1 pilocytic astrocytoma) treated with oral rapamycin, followed by serial MRI
data.finding: Five people with tuberous sclerosis complex whose brain astrocytomas were growing on serial scans (four subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, one pilocytic astrocytoma) were treated with oral rapamycin at standard immunosuppressive levels (blood 5-15 ng/ml) for 2.5 to 20 months. On MRI, every lesion shrank, and one showed necrosis. In one patient the tumour grew back when treatment was interrupted and shrank again when it was restarted. Treatment was well tolerated. This small uncontrolled series was one of the early reports that mTOR inhibition can shrink TSC brain tumours in patients, and it preceded the EXIST-1 everolimus trial. Boundary: 5 patients, open-label case series without a control group; TSC-associated astrocytomas only; regression depended on continued treatment.
data.abstract_excerpt: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder characterized by the formation of hamartomas in multiple organs. Five to 15% of affected individuals display subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, which can lead to substantial neurological and postoperative morbidity due to the production of hydrocephalus, mass effect, and their typical location adjacent to the foramen of Monro. We sought to see whether therapy with oral rapamycin could affect growth or induce regression in astrocytomas associated with TSC.

extracted_findings.effect: Regression of all 5 TSC-associated astrocytomas; regrowth on interruption, re-regression on resumption
